   Bonds, making headlines for the wrong reason recently, have been sinking for years. Incredibly, a dollar invested in the S&P 500, the most-followed stock index, would have more than doubled since the start of 2021 but lost value in the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index, the leading fixed-income benchmark.

   When stocks have had a really bad run, someone will always claim they saw it coming and that the signs were obvious. Well, maybe, but bonds’ negative returns really were foreseeable.

   Despite that, parts of millions of people’s paychecks were dutifully invested in them based on cookie-cutter formulas. The percentage rises mechanically by age because bonds are in theory less risky. Vanguard’s popular Target Retirement 2025 Fund , aimed at those right around retirement age, has just over half of its assets in bonds while the 2065 version designed for people just entering the workforce has barely 8%. That means older savers got hit harder by bonds’ poor performance.

   The best retirement strategy for most people is usually the cheapest and simplest. It should work on autopilot, avoiding rash decisions that can be influenced by scary or exciting headlines.

   But you didn’t need to be a newshound to get spooked when 10-year U.S. Treasury notes yielded barely half a percent in 2020. You were already losing money after inflation, and you were going to lose a lot more when yields got back to normal. Low coupon bonds have higher duration and greater convexity—measures of their price sensitivity to interest rates.

   That’s all water under the bridge, and things look very different today. There’s an argument that investors should now tilt away from stocks to bonds in those formulas given the multidecade highs in yields and lofty S&P 500 valuations.

   One measure that captures the trade-off is economist Robert Shiller’s Excess CAPE Yield. This compares the yield on stocks (the inverse of his cyclically adjusted P/E ratio) with inflation-adjusted bond yields. The difference between the two, stocks’ excess, is a low 1.01 percentage points today versus 4.88 percentage points in March 2020.

   So, in theory, the cookie-cutter approach that hurt older savers could help them today. Or maybe not, since future inflation is a wild card and it could dent bonds’ value more than real assets like stocks. One way to get the best of both worlds—a hands-off portfolio that tries to account for that math—might be an asset-allocation fund. 

   These have dynamic formulas. One is Bridgewater’s All Weather ETF , which is heavily overweight inflation-linked bonds. Another is Elm Wealth’s much cheaper Market Navigator ETF . It’s underweight both U.S. stocks and bonds at the moment, giving more weight to cash and emerging-market stocks.

   There are no guarantees in life—there could be wars, financial crises, or worse . But a portfolio that runs the numbers and accounts for what has done well or poorly when conditions were similar in the past could smooth that future path.

A better mousetrap?

 

“Set it and forget it” can be a solid investing strategy. Just don’t forget math.

 

Bonds, making headlines for the wrong reason recently, have been sinking for years. Incredibly, a dollar invested in the S&P 500, the most-followed stock index, would have more than doubled since the start of 2021 but lost value in the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index, the leading fixed-income benchmark.

 

When stocks have had a really bad run, someone will always claim they saw it coming and that the signs were obvious. Well, maybe, but bonds’ negative returns really were foreseeable.

 

Despite that, parts of millions of people’s paychecks were dutifully invested in them based on cookie-cutter formulas. The percentage rises mechanically by age because bonds are in theory less risky. Vanguard’s popular Target Retirement 2025 Fund, aimed at those right around retirement age, has just over half of its assets in bonds while the 2065 version designed for people just entering the workforce has barely 8%. That means older savers got hit harder by bonds’ poor performance.

 

The best retirement strategy for most people is usually the cheapest and simplest. It should work on autopilot, avoiding rash decisions that can be influenced by scary or exciting headlines.

 

But you didn’t need to be a newshound to get spooked when 10-year U.S. Treasury notes yielded barely half a percent in 2020. You were already losing money after inflation, and you were going to lose a lot more when yields got back to normal. Low coupon bonds have higher duration and greater convexity—measures of their price sensitivity to interest rates.

 

That’s all water under the bridge, and things look very different today. There’s an argument that investors should now tilt away from stocks to bonds in those formulas given the multidecade highs in yields and lofty S&P 500 valuations.

 

One measure that captures the trade-off is economist Robert Shiller’s Excess CAPE Yield. This compares the yield on stocks (the inverse of his cyclically adjusted P/E ratio) with inflation-adjusted bond yields. The difference between the two, stocks’ excess, is a low 1.01 percentage points today versus 4.88 percentage points in March 2020.

 

So, in theory, the cookie-cutter approach that hurt older savers could help them today. Or maybe not, since future inflation is a wild card and it could dent bonds’ value more than real assets like stocks. One way to get the best of both worlds—a hands-off portfolio that tries to account for that math—might be an asset-allocation fund. 

 

These have dynamic formulas. One is Bridgewater’s All Weather ETF, which is heavily overweight inflation-linked bonds. Another is Elm Wealth’s much cheaper Market Navigator ETF. It’s underweight both U.S. stocks and bonds at the moment, giving more weight to cash and emerging-market stocks.

 

There are no guarantees in life—there could be wars, financial crises, or worse. But a portfolio that runs the numbers and accounts for what has done well or poorly when conditions were similar in the past could smooth that future path.
